reliability_notes: The data are synthetic and generated by hand-written rules, so the model partly rediscovers those rules; scores here say little about how it would behave on real patients.

Test examples from the same patient are correlated (about 174 examples per patient, only 50 test patients), so examples are not independent and the test metrics are less certain than the example count suggests. There are no confidence intervals.
Missed doses are the minority class: 20.3% of training and 21.5% of test examples. Always predicting 'taken' would already score 78.5% accuracy on the test set, so accuracy alone is misleading.

At the 0.5 probability threshold the selected model finds 42.5% of missed doses (recall) with 69.3% precision, which is low recall for the minority class; the 0.3 and 0.6 risk bands are prototype values and were not tuned against these results.
Probabilities were not calibrated and no calibration check was done, so a displayed probability should not be read as a literal frequency.

Training uses knowledge time = the target dose's scheduled time. In the app the knowledge time can be earlier than the next dose (for example the 14:00 cohort snapshot), so the most recent doses may still be unresolved there; in the training data the previous dose is always resolved by the time the next one is due, so the model has not seen that situation.
The saved model is fitted on the training patients only (80% of patients); the held-out patients were not used to fit it, so the test numbers come from a single split (random_state=42).
The cross-validation gap between the two candidates (0.0014) is smaller than the fold-to-fold spread (0.0209), so the choice of model is not strongly supported.
selection_reason: Higher mean ROC-AUC in 5-fold patient-grouped cross-validation on training patients (0.781 vs 0.779).
target: Probability that the patient's next scheduled dose is missed (not taken within 120 minutes of the scheduled time).
